payload.name: Goal and aspiration retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks about a person's goals, aims, aspirations, career plans, or ambitions beyond their main field, and the initial search returns vague or partial results.
content: Run a structured predicate search for the subject with goal, aim, aspiration, plan, ambition, and endorsement predicates; do not restrict memory_kinds to profile/state—include preference and event memories.

Query specific goal categories (endorsements, charity, brand building, business ventures) when the question concerns non-primary ambitions; exclude goals in other domains unless the question asks broadly.
Before answering, verify each claimed goal is directly supported by a retrieved memory; if not, search with goal-relevant synonyms (improve, win, achieve, aspire, want).

payload.name: Exhaustive activity and item enumeration
payload.description: When a question asks for a list, set, or count of named items, categories, places, activities, or submission targets, retrieve all distinct instances instead of stopping at the first top-k.
content: Do not finalize from one generic search; run multiple queries pairing the person's name with synonym/category variants (outdoor activities, water sports, winter sports, travel, reading, art, fitness).

Use structured search (subject=<Person>) with predicates like activity, hobby, interest, plan, experience across event, preference, and profile memory kinds; avoid anchoring on an excluded/core activity when the question says 'besides' or 'other than'.

For items tied to a practice (e.g., yoga), expand to related contexts (meditation, relaxation, mindfulness) and treat recommendation/preference memories for those related activities as evidence; search item synonyms (album, track, playlist).

Verify each item is explicitly tied to the person, prefer the most specific form named, separate confirmed items from tentative/intention ones, and continue searching until all distinct items are collected.
For 'how many times' questions, search each inflected form and count distinct event records; prefer completed event memories over plan/intention memories for past-tense questions.

Before answering, verify each distinct item in the final answer has supporting memory; if coverage is missing, run a targeted query for that item. State incompleteness or plan-only evidence rather than implying completion. For ordinal questions (e.g., 'third screenplay'), search synonyms for the work type and achievement phrasing ('completed', 'finished', 'wrote'), look for ordinal indicators ('first', 'second', 'next', 'another'), and do not answer from a title-only memory unless it explicitly links the ordinal or is the only work of that type. For ordinal recurring events (e.g., 'first marathon', 'second trip'), do not limit retrieval to queries with the ordinal; search for the event type using synonyms and multiple modes, collect all memories of that event type (including those without ordinal labels), sort chronologically using explicit dates or relative time expressions, select the event at the requested ordinal position, and verify it describes the same event kind. If fewer events than the ordinal, state insufficient evidence rather than substituting another event. For inspiration questions, search discovery verbs (discovered, found, came across, read about, learned) around the work's creation date; do not answer with themes/plot unless explicitly stated as inspiration. If no explicit evidence, answer 'No information available'.

payload.name: Hobby/interest profile for context questions
payload.description: When a question uses hobbies/interests as explanation, theme, advice, recommendation, alternative career, or keep-busy during a period, and literal-term search misses the real answer.
content: Always run a hobby/interest profile search for the person: '<Person> hobbies and interests', '<Person> enjoys', or structured subject=<Person> with predicates interest/hobby, even if the initial search returns literal matches.

Treat the profile as evidence for why someone delayed/skipped, what keeps them busy, what they would advise, what hobby to recommend, or what theme is emerging; search concrete behaviors (helping, rescuing, traveling) for abstract-theme questions.

For alternative-career questions, explicitly exclude the primary domain (e.g., '<Person> non-gaming interests') and include hobbies, pet care, volunteering, and other non-professional activities as valid evidence.

When recommending or inferring, find intersections between the anchor interest and the person's demonstrated skills/hobbies (e.g., travel + writing = travel blog); attribute suggestions only to the persons whose memories support them.

payload.name: Teaching/helping concrete topic search
payload.description: When a question asks what skills a person taught/shared or the specific topic of help/challenge, and retrieved memories are vague or use different wording.
content: Expand the query without the literal word 'skills/help': use 'shared tips on', 'taught others to', 'showed others how to', 'helped others improve at', 'mentored', 'advised'; search social and event memories.

If a memory says only 'reached out for help with her challenges' or similar, do not guess the topic; run a follow-up search with requester name plus 'struggling', 'challenge', 'managing', 'needs help' and the date range.
Before finalizing, require at least one retrieved memory that explicitly names the taught skill or help topic; if absent, continue searching with synonym variants rather than inferring.

payload.name: Origin and trigger event retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks how someone started or was introduced to an activity, or why they made a decision, and initial search returns current events instead of the origin or cause.
content: For origin/introduction questions, expand with 'since childhood', 'started playing', 'began', 'first started', 'grew up', 'first experience with'; deliberately retrieve long-horizon preference/enrichment/state memories and look for family or mentor references.

For why-decision questions, after initial retrieval check for a precipitating life event (job loss, move, loss, career change); if none, search with causal terms filtered to the period just before the decision.

Use structured search for event or employment-status predicates when semantic search misses the cause; before answering, ensure a memory explicitly explains the origin or trigger; otherwise report it is absent.

payload.name: Broaden memory kinds for plan/location/duration questions
payload.description: When a question asks about plans, scheduled activities, a person's location during a period, duration of ownership, or what two people planned to do together instead of a named activity, do not restrict retrieval to event memories; include plan, travel, and profile/state memories and inspect timestamps.
content: If the question asks about future plans, scheduled activities, whereabouts during a date range, or how long someone has had/owned something, do not set memory_kinds=['event']; include 'plan', 'event', 'state', 'profile' or omit the filter.
Add query variants with plan/travel wording ('planned', 'scheduled', 'traveled to', 'visited', 'stayed in', 'trip to') and, for ownership/duration, 'has had', 'owned', 'kept for'.

When a range/date is given, prefer memories whose world_start/world_end falls inside the range even if their kind is plan/travel or profile/state; a planned trip or ownership duration is valid evidence for location/date questions. For ongoing activity (reading/working) include state AND event kinds; for projects/initiatives/goals include plan AND event with predicate project/initiative/goal; for miss/longing search exact predicates 'misses/longs for' and prefer preference/state.
Before concluding no information, rerun with the broader kind set and plan/travel/location keywords if the first range search only returned non-location events.

For visited places search event memories with indirect phrases: took a photo in, attended in, stayed in, was in, went to. For recent participation search concrete verbs: participated, presented, attended, spoke at, joined, plus artifact nouns (conference, workshop).
When 'recently' is asked, sort by world_start descending and filter to event kind. Inspect full content of compound memories; activities may be embedded rather than in headline.

Do not treat plans, stories, interests, or another person's actions as performed/present experiences. For habitual-activity-place questions, follow up with location synonyms (spot, nearby, area, goes to) and prefer a present-tense memory over a future plan.

For 'instead of' questions, after initial search, run an additional hybrid/keyword search using the two people plus generic plan terms like 'plan', 'together', 'play', 'activity' without repeating the replaced activity.

If results are still dominated by the replaced activity, search profile/enrichment memories about the person's interests or shared activities and inspect full content; the alternative may be embedded there.
Do not finalize based on a plausible trip or retreat memory; prefer explicit evidence of what the pair planned together, and cite that memory instead of inferring.

payload.name: Time-window synonym and relative-time retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks what a person did, visited, started, or how many times/places within a named period, expand action verbs with synonyms, apply structured world_start/world_end filters, and include relative-time expressions before answering 'no information'.
content: Extract subject, activity type, and time range; expand activity terms with synonyms (travel: trip, road trip, visit, vacation, went to; classes: took, joined, started, attended, enrolled in). For 'after an event' questions, set window to [event_date, +2 days]; for 'recently' with anchor date, use [date−14, date]; for named period, use that period.

Run structured searches filtering memory_kind 'event'/'plan' with world_start/world_end overlapping the range, plus hybrid/keyword searches using each synonym and relative-time phrases ('last week', 'a few days ago', 'recently') anchored to the current date.

A memory is relevant if its stored world_start/world_end falls in the requested period, even if its text uses relative time or lacks the literal month/date; treat activity-at-location memories (retreat in Phuket) as travel/presence evidence.
For counts or 'which places', enumerate all matching memories and answer with all distinct supported items; only say 'No information' after all synonym and structured searches fail.
If windowed search yields only generic/no named item, rerun WITHOUT time filter to surface concrete names; report item but don't assert the specific date unless another memory confirms.

payload.name: Concrete-term and co-referent expansion
payload.description: When a question describes an abstract change, personal milestone, post-event plan, or a person under an alternate name (nickname, typo, alternate spelling) and the initial search with literal/abstract wording returns nothing, re-query with concrete observable terms, co-referent role words, or name variants before concluding no information.
content: If direct search with the abstract/role wording fails (e.g., 'physical transformation', 'future wife', 'after the networking event'), build queries from concrete terms likely in the memory: 'dyed hair', 'haircut', 'tattoo' for changes; 'met', 'met a woman', 'trip' for milestones; named business actions for post-event plans.

Run subject-scoped searches (subject=person, memory_kind=event/plan); after an event memory is found, retrieve other memories with the same subject and same/nearby world date—post-event plans often share that timestamp. If no post-event action is found, search for the same subject with world_start equal to the anchor's date (or ±1 day) and inspect the anchor memory's version with sources to find other memories from the same source/turn; treat a same-timestamp memory as strong evidence for 'after' only if it describes an action plausibly following the event.
For 'when' questions, use world_start of candidate event memories and interpret relative time words; do not require an explicit date string in the memory.
Only answer 'No information' after concrete-expanded and subject-scoped searches return no plausible match.

If the subject may appear under a different name (nickname, shortened, misspelled, alternate spelling), identify variants from memory or conversation context and re-run the search with each variant plus original keywords; filter by the alternative subject name if structured search is available.
Check whether candidate memories under alternate names match the time/event/context; include them as evidence if they refer to the same person.

payload.name: EmotionStressorConcreteAndSynonymSearch
payload.description: When a question asks about a person's or pair's frustration, stressor, shared experience, or similar emotion and initial search with the abstract term returns weak results.
content: Expand abstract emotion terms with synonyms and concrete context: for 'frustration' use 'stressful', 'cannot find', 'blocked goal'; for 'stressor' include 'stress', 'pressure', 'tough', 'worried'. Search person's name plus concrete objects from the question.

For shared experiences between two named people, run separate queries per person using the concrete object (e.g., 'Andrew pet-friendly spot', 'Bella inability to find housing'); treat a blocked-goal event as evidence of the shared experience even if the emotion word is absent.

For recurring frustrations, combine the person's name with the concrete object and frequency indicators: 'weekly', 'every week', 'constantly', 'repeatedly'. Verify with a follow-up search that another memory confirms recurrence.

If the question excludes a factor (e.g., 'besides hiking'), remove that term from the query and search the active domain (work, family, health); require explicit connection of the person to the emotion before answering.

For avoidance/put-off/skipped questions, search the person's competing activities and preferences during the period; never answer with memories that only explain why they do/enjoy the activity. Accept only memories that explicitly connect the activity to the outcome/emotion (e.g., 'feels happiness through', 'is her go-to stress relief'); do not infer emotion from passion/traits or use engagement reasons for avoidance; otherwise answer 'No information available'.

payload.name: Conjunctive question facet search
payload.description: When a question asks for an activity or object satisfying multiple constraints about the same subject and the initial joint search returns evidence for only one constraint.
content: Parse the question into separate constraints (facets). For 'indoor activity Andrew enjoys while making his dog happy', facets are (a) an activity Andrew enjoys, (b) an activity relating to his dog.
Run independent searches per facet: for enjoyment search 'Andrew hobbies', 'activities Andrew enjoys'; for dog search 'Andrew's dog', 'activities with dog'. Do not rely on one combined query.
If one facet is under-represented in initial results, explicitly search that facet before answering. Do not accept a candidate that only satisfies one facet.
Intersect results: find an item supported by at least one memory per facet, e.g., one showing Andrew enjoys cooking and another showing he has a dog and cares about it.

payload.name: Per-subject coverage for multi-person questions
payload.description: When a question asks about attributes, events, methods, or shared interests of multiple named people and the initial combined search covers only some of them, or when a single similarity query returns only relationship memories and misses parallel life-event memories.
content: Identify every named person; run a dedicated search per person using the person's name plus the relevant topic, with synonyms/paraphrases (e.g., 'practice', 'sessions', 'routine' for yoga).

For shared interests, retrieve each person's profile/preference memories separately (terms: 'interest', 'hobby', 'enjoys') and intersect; a common interest exists if both have supporting memories, even without a joint activity.
For methods/techniques, search preference-kind memories with sensory/environmental vocabulary (e.g., 'candles', 'music', 'calm atmosphere') to surface per-person method memories.

If the question implies multiple instances per person (plural events), issue additional query variants to surface more memories; before answering, verify every named person has at least one supporting memory, otherwise continue searching or state unavailability.

For 'what do X and Y have in common' questions, run a separate search for each person combining their name with event concepts (e.g., 'job', 'lost job', 'business', 'started', 'founded', 'career'). Compare predicates across retrieved memories; if both share analogous predicates (e.g., both 'lost job', both 'started a business'), treat matched pairs as the answer even without an explicit relationship memory. If a similarity query returns only relationship/support memories, do not accept it; rerun per-person event searches until parallel pairs are found or evidence shows none exist.
For 'what A did/described/shared with B', if A-anchored search misses B, run a second search with B as subject plus shared/activity terms ('mentioned', 'excited about', 'play with A').
For 'what do A and B have in common', do a per-person comparison of life-situation attributes (job, business, etc.); never treat one person's support for the other as a commonality.
Require a memory that explicitly names the activity/plan linking both people or names the common attribute for both; otherwise answer 'No information available' rather than inferring.

payload.name: Multi-person recommendation grounding
payload.description: When a question asks for a gift, recommendation, or activity for multiple named people, especially tied to health/lifestyle changes, and initial search returns only generic profile memories.
content: Expand the recommendation purpose into concrete candidate categories (e.g., for healthy lifestyle: cookbook, cooking class, meal delivery, gym equipment, running gear, diet plan).
Run structured searches filtered to memory_kind 'event' and 'preference' for each person to surface recent classes, hobbies, meals, and plans that may inspire the recommendation.
Search for memories connecting the people (shared events, recipes, plans, mutual interests) and treat those shared connections as primary evidence for the recommendation.

Before finalizing, verify each named person has at least one supporting memory or a memory mentioning both. If missing, run follow-up searches derived from retrieved memories (e.g., if cooking, search 'cookbook recipe').

payload.name: Relax Overly Strict Time and Actor Filters
payload.description: When a question names a date/month but the core evidence is a subject/action memory outside that exact point, or 'shared with' wrongly requires both names, widen time windows and drop actor constraints.
content: Parse month/year mentions as ranges (first to last day) using time_mode 'range'; never treat a month as a single point date.
When the date seems approximate or the subject/action match is strong, relax the time filter by at least ±3 months and prefer the matching memory, noting its actual date.
For 'shared/told with Y in period', do not require Y or both names in the memory; query with the sharer X as subject and event/action terms.

payload.name: Holiday Season Event Mapping
payload.description: When a question asks which holiday season coincided with a person's event and no memory mentions the holiday, retrieve event memories and map their world_start dates to calendar holiday windows.
content: Identify the person and event type from the question; then run a structured search for memories with subject = person and memory_kind = 'event', using semantic variants if needed.
For each event memory with a world_start date, map it to standard holiday windows (Christmas: late Nov–Dec; New Year: Jan 1; Thanksgiving: late Nov; Halloween: Oct 31).
Answer with the holiday season containing the event date; if multiple matches, prefer the most recent event satisfying the question's semantics.

payload.name: Direct Authorship Evidence Over Preferences
payload.description: When a question asks what a person writes, creates, or is working on and initial retrieval returns only reading or liking memories, search for direct authorship evidence.
content: Treat retrieval as provisional; scan for direct authorship phrases: 'X is working on', 'X is writing', 'X wrote', 'X published', 'X's novel/story/article'.
If only preference/reading memories appear, run additional keyword search with 'writing', 'working on', 'novel', 'story', 'plot', 'author', 'article' plus the person's name, and increase top_k.
Look for event memories describing recent writing activities, challenges, plot elements, or completed works; they reveal genre/content.
Base final answer on direct authorship evidence; use preferences only as supporting context, never alone.

payload.name: Concrete Keepsake Search for Memory Methods
payload.description: When a question asks how someone remembers or preserves memories, expand retrieval to concrete keepsake objects like corkboards, notebooks, photos, albums.
content: If the question asks how a person remembers/records happy moments, add keepsake object terms: corkboard, notebook, journal, diary, photo, album, scrapbook, letter, combined with the person's name.
Run a second search using these object terms; do not dismiss a memory merely because it mentions the object in passing.
Include memories about these objects as candidate memory-retention methods in the answer, even without the word 'remember'.

payload.name: Attribute Retrieval with Contextual Inference
payload.description: When a question asks for a factual attribute (age, breed, job, etc.) of a person, pet, or possession, and initial retrieval returns no direct statement or only unrelated/tangential memories, retrieve this skill.
content: Do not restrict searches to memory_kind 'state'; include 'event' and other kinds since attributes often appear in event statements (e.g., 'owns two cats, Luna (5yo)').
If the entity is a pet or possession, also search by the owner's name and by any known sub-entity names (pet names) paired with attribute synonyms (breed/mix/age/color).

After one failed search, run semantic/hybrid searches with inferred life-stage or role terms (school, student, finals, job, partner, retired) instead of literal attribute words. For problem/challenge questions, replace abstract terms with concrete difficulty markers (tough, hard, difficult, struggled, couldn't, unable to, looking/trying to find, contacting) plus person's name and goal entity; run at least two distinct query formulations. For age/life-stage questions, after a direct search of 'age/years old/birthday' fails, search the person's name with life-stage terms (student, school, studying, finals, internship, university, college, graduated, working).
Before answering, verify you are using the latest version of each evidence memory; inspect memories whose topic seems unrelated (e.g., routine, favorite spots) for embedded attribute values.

For both problem and age/life-stage questions, include memory_kind event, plan, and preference (not only state); accept evidence only if explicit (difficulty marker or life-stage fact) — never infer the attribute from neutral activity; if expanded searches fail, answer 'No information available'.

payload.name: Preference-First Retrieval for Recommendations
payload.description: When a question asks what a person suggested, recommended, or considers ideal for an item or another person, and 'recommend'/'suggest' searches return no support, expand to preference/hobby memories and verify evidence.
content: Parse the question into subject (person), object/item, any attribute (e.g., calming), and any recipient (for 'recommend to'). Identify the item category (game, book, movie, etc.).

First search explicit terms: 'recommended', 'suggested', 'ideal'. If no memory shows subject endorsing the item, query '<subject> enjoys/likes/favorite <item>' and '<subject> preferences for <item>'. For recipient questions, use recommender's preferences, not recipient's actions.

For ideal/opinion questions, decompose item into attributes (location, lighting, materials, atmosphere) and search '<subject> <attribute> <item>'; include structured search filtered to memory_kind='preference' if available.

Verify memory supports claim: right subject, predicate, object, attribute. Don't use activity/event memories as preferences; prefer items listed as subject's general enjoyment/hobby over unrelated contexts.

For fan/favorite questions only (not authorship/creating), if no memory names the item, rerun with person plus preference terms: 'favorite', 'likes', 'enjoys', 'loves', 'is a fan of', and category. Skip if already directly named.

For 'what A recommended to B' questions, if recipient-inclusive search finds no support, rerun with A plus recommendation words ('recommended', 'suggested', 'advised') and item type, without B. Do not apply when direct evidence already exists.

For adjective-laden recommendation questions with no direct endorsement, rerun without adjectives (name + recommendation verbs + category) and search preference/hobby memories for an explicit 'recommends' list.

Run structured/kind-filtered searches over preference, profile/enrichment, and event memories (predicates favorite, likes, recommends) and inspect full content; only abstain if no memory explicitly links the item. Never infer from closest matches or adjectives.

payload.name: Enumerate Group Members and Loss Euphemisms
payload.description: When a question asks who in a group (family, team, friends) was injured, died, passed, lost, or involved, or enumerates relationship categories like 'family and friends'; also when initial search returns only the main subject, or when direct friend searches return only known relationships and the question asks about friends, teammates, colleagues, or other contacts beyond a named person.
content: Expand queries with relationship terms and euphemistic loss words: 'lost', 'grieving', 'in memory of', 'late', 'passed away', 'deceased' — especially for death/loss questions.

Enumerate every likely group member or relationship category, then run a separate targeted hybrid/BM25 search for each pairing the member/category with the event or attribute in the question (e.g., 'Evan's son injury', 'his friend lost').
Increase retrieval depth: use top_k 15-20 or structured filters (subject=main subject, predicates related to injury/death/health/event) to surface memories beyond the main subject.
Before answering, verify each relationship category or member has supporting evidence; if any is missing, search further rather than finalizing an incomplete answer.

If direct friend searches return only known relationships or nothing, search for the person's group activities and memberships using terms like 'team', 'tournament', 'club', 'league', 'competition', 'participated', 'joined', 'group', 'band', 'company', 'project'. Treat any memory of team-based, competitive, or collaborative activity as support for having teammates/peers beyond the named friend.

payload.name: Health Condition Synonym Search
payload.description: When a question asks about a person's allergies, ailments, or medical conditions, or when initial search returns only generic risk or a single allergen category.
content: Run searches with both literal and related terms: allergy, allergen, intolerant, intolerance, dairy-free, gluten-free, avoid, can't eat, sensitive, reaction, health issue, medical condition, ailment, disease, diagnosis.
Treat memories of dietary restrictions, avoidance behaviors, or generic health risks as evidence toward a specific condition; include them in the evidence list.

If the question expects a named condition/ailment, verify a specific name was found. If memory contains only generic risk/weight statements, continue searching (e.g., structured health_issue predicate) or return low confidence.
If initial results cover only one allergen category (e.g., animal/fur), explicitly search food-related terms (dairy, nut, shellfish, gluten) to capture other allergens.

payload.name: Motto Paraphrase Retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks about a motto, slogan, saying, quote, catchphrase, family value, or symbolic phrase attributed to a person or family, and direct keyword search fails, retrieve paraphrased expressions.
content: Search using the full question as a query via semantic or hybrid retrieval, not just exact terms like 'motto'.
Expand query with synonyms: 'motto', 'saying', 'quote', 'catchphrase', 'slogan', 'phrase', 'sign', 'symbol', 'family value', 'togetherness', plus the person's name or pronoun.
Inspect candidate memories about objects, signs, travel, or symbols for phrases like 'read', 'serves as', 'means to us', or 'emphasizes' that indicate the motto.
Declare 'No information available' only after at least one semantic search and one synonym-expanded keyword search both fail.

payload.name: Promotion-Tactic Multi-Search
payload.description: When a question asks how someone promoted, marketed, advertised, or grew a business or brand, run multiple tactic-based searches because one generic 'promote' query often retrieves partial evidence.
content: Do not answer after a single 'promote' or 'marketing' search; promotion memories often use concrete tactic words instead.

Run targeted queries: 'ad campaign', 'advertisement', 'collaboration', 'partnership', 'limited edition', 'video presentation', 'demo', 'social media', 'event', 'offer', 'discount', 'promotion', 'launch', 'showcase', 'styling'.
Use structured search if available: subject = person, predicate in ['action', 'activity', 'business'], object containing store/business terms; inspect recent event memories for business activities.
Merge unique results, check breadth of distinct tactics, and search synonyms once more if a new tactic is found.

payload.name: Reading/Viewing Consumption Evidence
payload.description: When a question asks what books/movies/shows a person read/finished/is watching and initial search returns only interests or generic descriptions, search for explicit consumption statements across event, preference, and enrichment memories.
content: For reading/viewing consumption questions, search person + verbs: 'has read', 'is reading', 'finished', 'reread', 'currently watching', 'just finished reading'; include event, preference, and enrichment memory kinds.
Inspect full content, not just headlines, for explicit quoted titles; compound memories (e.g., 'mentioned he is reading X and found it gripping') are direct evidence.

Treat only explicit consumption statements as evidence for 'has read' questions; interest, recommendation, genre description is not sufficient. For 'just finished', use preference/enrichment memories with relative-time phrases like 'recently finished reading'.

payload.name: Anchor-relative date retrieval windows
payload.description: When a question uses a date anchor with ordering wording (weekday before/after, before/after travel), search a window or the correct side of the anchor instead of a single computed date.
content: For 'the [weekday] before/after <date>' questions, never set time_mode=point on the computed weekday; use time_mode range from anchor-7 to anchor+1 so both the weekday and the anchor date are covered. Do NOT apply to exact-date lookups like 'on July 24'.

For 'which city before/after traveling to <destination>' questions, first retrieve the travel event and use its world_start as anchor, then search location-bearing memories (event, plan, future event, travel, state) dated strictly on the required side and verify each candidate's date.
If no memory falls on the correct side/window, answer 'No information available'; never substitute a city or event from the wrong side or a co-occurring mention.

payload.name: Plan memory retrieval with correct date semantics
payload.description: When a question asks when/what someone is planning for a relative future period or intends a future event, search plan-kind memories and treat their world_start as the record date, not the event date.
content: When the question uses planning language ('planning', 'intends', 'scheduled', 'next summer'), include memory_kind 'plan' and do not restrict to 'event'. Do not put target_time range filters on plan memories: their world_start records when the plan was made, not the planned event.

For relative future phrases ('next summer', 'next year'), read the plan memory's content and check it explicitly names the event and relative period; compute the calendar period from the record date, never invent a specific date.

Do not accept a candidate of a different event type (e.g., get-together for reunion). If no plan/event memory explicitly matches the requested event, answer 'No information available' rather than substituting a similar memory.

payload.name: Residence proximity via event memories
payload.description: When a question asks whether someone lives near a geographic feature and profile/state search found no residence, search event memories with feature vocabulary before answering 'No information available'.
content: Include memory kinds 'event' (and 'plan' only for future stays) when searching 'lives near beach/sea/mountains/lake/river'; do not restrict to profile/state. If a profile/state memory already states residence, rely on it instead.

Run a hybrid/keyword search pairing the person's name with the feature and synonyms plus place-them-there verbs: 'sat by', 'walked along', 'went to', 'visited', 'stayed at', 'lives near', 'grew up by'.
Use only present/near-present memories as evidence; do not use a distant holiday/travel memory. If no event memory places the person at the feature, answer 'No information available'.

payload.name: Explicit visit evidence for visited cities
payload.description: When a question asks which cities/places a person has visited or been to, require direct visit evidence and exclude recommendation-only mentions and country-level results.
content: Only use for 'has visited/been to/traveled to' enumeration questions; for 'recommended/favorite/must-visit' use recommendation-specific search instead.

Run hybrid/keyword search with the person's name and visit verbs: 'visited', 'traveled to', 'went to', 'has been to', 'stayed in', 'was in', 'game in', 'trip to', 'will visit'; include event, plan, activity, travel kinds; inspect full memory content for embedded city mentions.

Include a place only when the memory explicitly connects the person to that place as a visit/trip/event. Exclude places that appear only as recommendations or another person's actions. For city-level questions, do not list country/region places. If no direct visit memory exists, answer 'No information available'.

payload.name: Food and recipe preference search
payload.description: When a question asks which food/meat category a person prefers or what meal/dish they cook, and literal category or appliance-term searches return no dish, search preference/profile memories for named dishes/recipes before saying unavailable.
content: Include preference and profile memory kinds when a question asks which food/meat category a person prefers or what dish/meal they cook; skip this skill if a direct '<Person> favorite <category>' memory already answers or the question is a direct lookup of a named dish.

Search '<Person> favorite dish/recipe/meal', 'loves', 'go-to', '<ingredient> dish'; if an appliance (slow cooker) anchors the query, rerun without it using 'cooks', 'enjoys cooking', 'favorite recipe'. Inspect compound preference memories for a named dish.

Map a named dish to a category only when the category term appears literally in the memory text (e.g., 'Roasted Chicken' identifies chicken); never infer ingredients or recipe from the dish name or co-occurring memories.
If no retrieved memory names the category/dish, answer 'No information available'; event/activity/pet memories are not food-preference evidence and must not be used to guess.

payload.name: Multi-person practice enhancement methods
payload.description: When a question asks ways two or more people enhance/improve a recurring practice (yoga, meditation, workout), search concrete tool/atmosphere terms and preference memories, verifying explicit evidence for every named person.
content: Trigger only for 'what ways do two or more people enhance/improve their [recurring practice]?' (yoga, meditation, workout); do not use for one-off event or scheduling questions.

Don't rely on the literal word 'enhance' or event memories. Also search each person with concrete practice-enhancement terms: candles, music, essential oils, incense, props, lighting, calming, peaceful, atmosphere; include preference/state memory kinds.
If initial search misses a named person, run follow-up '<name> <practice> <tool/atmosphere synonyms>' and ensure every named person's claimed enhancement has a retrieved memory.

Verify each claimed tool is explicit in the correct person's memory; otherwise report 'No information available' for that person. Never infer from co-occurring activities or another person's memories.

payload.name: Symbolic object purpose retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks why a person decided to get/keep a meaningful object and object-name searches return no memory, search semantic/function vocabulary for symbolic motivation before saying unavailable.
content: Trigger only for 'why did Person decide to get/keep [meaningful object]?'; do not apply to factual attributes (identity, date, cost), which require the object name in retrieved memories.

If object-name search returns nothing, search semantic/function vocabulary with the person: 'motivated by', 'symbolizes', 'represents', 'reminds', 'strength', 'resilience', 'tough times', 'inspires', 'means to him'; include event and state memory kinds.

A memory is support only if it explicitly states the person's symbolic/motivational purpose. If it explains motivation without naming the question's object, answer with the stated motivation; never claim a memory names the object unless it does.
If no memory explicitly explains a symbolic purpose, answer 'No information available'; do not generalize from unrelated memories.

payload.name: Career-high and record performance retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks for career-high, personal-best, record-breaking, or best-ever performances, often within a named year, and abstract superlative searches return partial or vague results, expand into concrete domain metrics and require explicit superlative wording.
content: Apply only to superlative-performance questions (career-high, personal best, record, best-ever). If the question names a specific statistic, treat as direct lookup and skip expansion.

Enumerate concrete performance metrics for the domain (basketball: points/assists/rebounds; other sports: goals/time/distance; professional: score/sales/rank) and run a search for each metric with the person, time range, and superlative synonyms ('highest', 'best', 'career-high', 'record', 'ever'). Do not finalize after one generic 'career-high' search.

Count a memory as career-high only if its text contains an explicit superlative qualifier ('highest ... ever', 'career-high', 'personal best', 'record'). Do not infer a record from a plain statistic or non-superlative match. If some claimed superlative cannot be found, state only supported items and say 'No information available' for the rest.

payload.name: Achievement predicate project inventory
payload.description: When a question asks for a plural inventory of a person's projects or accomplishments, and the first search returns only generic 'project' mentions, expand search to achievement predicates and verify each listed type.
content: Run additional searches pairing the person with achievement vocabulary: built, designed, developed, created, prototype, milestone, ambition, working on, plus field-specific object nouns. Do not use for single named project; search by name only.

Use structured search (subject=<Person>) across event/plan kinds with predicates accomplishment, project development, ambition, milestone, and activity, not only 'project'. Do not expand for preference/relationship/location questions.

Before finalizing, verify every listed project kind has a retrieved memory explicitly naming it. If unsupported, state 'No information available' rather than inferring. Do not apply to single-fact lookups.
